title: Why Does a Maglev Train Float?
description:
In Japan, a train has carried people at six hundred three kilometers an hour, faster than the takeoff speed of an airliner. And it did it without touching the ground. Maglev trains have no wheels on the rails at full speed. They float, held up by magnets, a few millimeters or a few centimeters above the track. Today, eleven parts of a floating train, and why each one exists.

Machine Reverse takes apart the machines you see every day and explains, part by part, why each one exists. This video covers 11 parts.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:15 1. The arms that hug the track
2:38 2. The 10 millimeter gap
4:00 3. The motor in the track
5:18 4. The frozen magnets
6:46 5. The wheels it still needs
8:08 6. The figure 8 coils
9:22 7. The track that bends
10:44 8. The guideway in the air
12:03 9. The line under the mountains
13:25 10. The lesson of Lathen
14:44 11. The shielded cabin
16:03 The verdict

Sources:
- Magnetic levitation basics, EMS vs EDS: Wikipedia, "Maglev" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maglev
- Transrapid (electromagnetic suspension, ~10 mm gap, bending switches, Emsland test facility): Wikipedia, "Transrapid" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transrapid
- Shanghai Maglev (2004, 30 km, 431 km/h): Wikipedia, "Shanghai maglev train" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_maglev_train
- SCMaglev (superconducting magnets, ~10 cm levitation, wheels below ~150 km/h, null-flux coils): Wikipedia, "SCMaglev" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SCMaglev and JR Central, "Superconducting Maglev" https://global.jr-central.co.jp/en/company/ir/annualreport/
- 603 km/h world record (21 April 2015): Guinness World Records, "Fastest maglev train" https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/fastest-maglev-train
- Linear motors and Linimo: Wikipedia, "Linimo" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linimo
- Chuo Shinkansen (Tokyo-Nagoya, delays, Shizuoka water dispute): Wikipedia, "Chūō Shinkansen" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C5%AB%C5%8D_Shinkansen
- Lathen train collision (22 September 2006, 23 deaths): Wikipedia, "Lathen train collision" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lathen_train_collision
